en: For truth, renunciation, tranquility, and wisdom are those qualities conducive to nirvāṇa;
and intelligence is the basis by which one presides over these.
Nirvāṇa itself is also said to be the three bases, beginning with truth.
Setting aside those two bases, however, the wise apply their intellect to all things.
(6.2) Because of that ethical discipline, some are equal to the Unequalled; others, whether having heard or not heard the truth, perceive it through investigation. (6.3)
Hearing, practicing recitation, reflecting upon the teaching,
and cultivating the signs of meditative concentrations, one proceeds upon the true path.
The perfection of love and reverence arises from the emergence of a sense of shame and dread of blame.
Those from whom you should serve as teachers—those Buddhas and their disciples—from the teachers comes the perfection of learning;
from learning comes the investigation of the meaning;
from the understanding of the meaning comes joy; and from joy arises gladness. (6.5–6)
From joy arises the perfection of pliancy; from pliancy, the birth of bliss;

from bliss, the emergence of meditative concentration; and from meditative concentration, the vision of reality. (6.7) From the vision of reality arises disenchantment; from disenchantment, dispassion; and from the arising of disenchantment, [liberation].

From dispassion comes liberation, and from liberation comes nirvāṇa. (6.8) The hearing of the discourse on truth should be known as "learning" (*śruta*); the reflection upon it is "investigation" (*vicāraṇa*).
The realization of its meaning is "correct discernment" (*samyaksantīraṇa*). (6.9)
In the sūtras, birth and so forth are suffering; craving is the origin of suffering;
the exhaustion of craving is nirvāṇa; and there is also the eightfold path.
These correspond respectively to that which possesses faults, the fault itself, the absence of faults, and that which destroys faults. (6.10 [217])
Some [assert that] the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path to nirvāṇa [are established as follows]:

(6.11) The three types of agreeable objects and so forth are suffering because they are corrupted by the three kinds of suffering; however, craving is the cause [of suffering] because it generates them, or else [the cause] is precisely those [agreeable objects]. (6.12)

Pure in ethical discipline, contented, with the senses well-restrained, delighting in solitary dwellings, and endowed with wisdom, energy, and mindfulness; then follows mindfulness of breathing in six or four ways, and thereafter the meditation on the foul. (6.13 [220])
Each application of mindfulness is threefold by way of its mode;
(6.14) it is considered that the applications of mindfulness consist of the body, feelings, mind, and the remaining phenomena, as the antidotes to the perversions. (6.15)
Through the investigation of the pure and the impure by way of substance and characteristic,

and through the sequence of impermanence, the counteracting of causes, and the departure [from saṃsāra], there arises what is called "receptivity" (kṣānti), which is both comprehensive and non-contradictory. (6.16)
The signs (*nimitta*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), as well as the sequence beginning with joy (*prāmodya*), are as follows:

(6.17) Thereafter, one perceives suffering through three knowledges; likewise, the remaining [truths] through three by three. One destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) here in two [stages] by means of the first and the third [knowledges]. (6.18)

Then, in the thirteenth moment of mind, the noble one attains the fruit; loathing them, he realizes that sensual desires are impure in two ways. In the second [moment], being greatly disenchanted, he attains the untainted fruit.
But the noble one, being entirely disenchanted, attains the third [fruit].
(6.20) Because of the total destruction of the afflictions that function through outward orientation, this is called detachment; beyond this, he is one who has transcended passion. (6.21)
Through the liberation from the fetters that operate inwardly,
he attains liberation and the fourth, stainless fruit.
This occurs through the cessation of the connection to existence produced by prior and subsequent transgressions.
Free from afflictions, one enters final nirvāṇa like a fire without fuel.
(6.23) Some are fixed in falsehood; others likewise remain in the undetermined state. Ordinary persons who have seen the truth remain fixed in the state of correctness. (6.24)
Two are established in the faculty of "I shall come to know"; three are established in the faculty of "knowing";
and two are established in the faculty of "one who has known. Thus, those seven are again [to be understood] as follows:
one who follows through faith is to be known as having dull faculties on the path of seeing.

The follower by dharma (dharmānusārī) is one of sharp faculties who remains established in that very state. These two—the one liberated through faith (śraddhāvimukta) and the one attained to vision (dṛkprāpta)—are established in the fruit; they should be known as those who have not yet attained liberation, while those who have attained it are the body-witnesses (kāyasākṣin).

The two Arhats liberated by wisdom are those who have not attained the liberations; however, those same two are liberated in both ways if they have attained them. Here, the two established in the fruits are the Stream-enterer and the Once-returner.
In the three [stages], the non-returner and the one beyond training [are distinguished] by the prior abandonment and the acquisition of another [fruit].
(6.29) And there are four candidates for the fruits respectively; the candidates for the fruit of once-returner and non-returner are considered to be of two kinds. (6.30)
One who has destroyed the three fetters is to be known as one who will be reborn at most seven times;
and by attenuating the passions, one who is reborn in this world for a third time is a *kulaṃkula*.
Furthermore, by thinning out the passions, one becomes a *sakṛdāgāmin* immediately thereafter.

Furthermore, through the destruction of most of those [fetters], he becomes a "single-seeded" one among humans or gods. (6.32) By abandoning five fetters, he is a Non-returner (anāgāmin), who is of five types:
one who flows upwards (ūrdhvasrotas), and those who attain nirvana with exertion (sasamskāra), without exertion (asamskāra), or in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin). (6.33)
This [attainment] is considered to be of three types due to differences in place and time:
the first goes to Akaniṣṭha; the next is that which is mixed within the dhyānas; and the following is the other [type].
There are also three others who go to the formless realms, but for one of these, nirvāṇa occurs here in this very life.
He is an Arhat who has completely exhausted all bonds of the afflictions;
furthermore, he is one capable of falling away, one capable of volitional effort, and likewise one capable of guarding [his attainment];
he is one stable and unshakable, and likewise one capable of penetrating the state of being immovable. (6.35–36)
These are liberated at all times; they have attained the knowledge of destruction.

The sixth is liberated both at times and not at times; he belongs to the immovable category and to that [category] as well. The first and the last are the stainless path, which continues until the eradication of the afflictions.
Up to that point, one is a learner (*śaikṣa*); beyond that, however, one should be known as a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and he is further classified in three ways.
He is designated by means of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), abandonments (*prahāṇa*), and faculties (*indriya*).
Among these, their mutual inferiority, equality, and superiority are established solely through their respective relations to one another.
The excellence of the faculties arises from lineage, cultivation, and abandonment;
and from these, as well as from the distinction of victory, comes the excellence of meditative attainment.
(6.40) For the abandonment of many is indeed superior to the abandonment of few.

Because of the direct excellence of abandonment, the liberations are not indistinguishable. (6.41) In brief, there are exactly three types of falling away: from the fruit, from the attainment of the path, and from abandonment; these concern what has been attained, what has not yet been attained, and enjoyment. (6.42)

When existence has been overturned, there is no falling away from what has been attained; for a noble one who has fallen away, death occurs—this is not a matter of dispute. (6.43) Through revulsion and dispassion toward material forms, liberation is realized.
Or, by means of both the defiled and undefiled paths, [abandonment occurs] even from the three formless realms.
(6.44) In the formless realm, the complete abandonment of what is to be abandoned by vision is effected only by the undefiled path; that which is mundane remains bound. (6.45)
The cause is for the abandonment of the path, not for the abandonment that is eternal;
another is for the full comprehension of both, while yet another is for neither. (6.46) In some cases, these two are realized through the body and likewise through wisdom.
The two paths to liberation are not obstructed by the factors of the path’s duration and so forth.
When cultivated, the paths indeed increase in strength;
the former is the cause of the latter, but that [latter] is not the cause of the former. (6.47–48)
For some paths, whether present or future, are cultivated;
those that destroy the afflictions, however, are either present or in the very process of perishing.
The former [type of path] is preceded by that [destruction], through the attainment of the fruit, while the latter is through falling away. (6.49)
The untainted path is abandoned, or else its abandonment occurs through a subsequent [path].

(6.50) An ordinary person does not attain the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing; nor do they attain the destruction of what is to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm, nor the stainless fruit. (6.51)
Faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
as well as joy, pliancy, equanimity, aspiration, intention, and restraint—these are designated as the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and the foundations of mindfulness. (6.52)
These are the faculties and the powers, as well as the factors of enlightenment and the true path.
Faith and resolve regarding the truths, as well as toward the Three Jewels, and the exertion of grasping when reflecting on the true nature of reality, is called vigor. (6.53–54)
In this very way, all qualities such as mindfulness and so forth are to be described.
There is also physical pliancy, while the aggregate of ethical discipline is restraint.
Whatever other such qualities exist in the applications toward wholesome states—
All those should be understood as being merely semblances of the factors conducive to awakening.
On the stage of vision, the path is primary; thereafter come the limbs of wisdom; on the stage of no-more-learning, however, the powers are primary, while the others are merely followers. (6.56–57)

Having recognized the diversity of the afflictions of those to be trained, the Self-Arisen Ones have proclaimed various teachings through various gateways for the sake of abandoning each respective affliction: the mind, the roots of virtue, and appropriate mental attention. (6.58) [265] The mind, the roots of virtue, and thorough reflection—

The causes of the factors conducive to awakening, as well as other stainless qualities, are wholesome and immaculate. Morality and pliancy are not associated with the mind; they have objects, are conjoined, and follow along with the mind. (6.59–60)
All coexistent immaterial factors, or karma, are not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

They are to be abandoned by insight (*dhiyā*), are knowable, and are considered to be of two kinds as objects of realization. Or else, all these combined exist entirely within the meditative absorption born of seclusion (*vivekaja-dhyāna*).
These should be understood as being devoid of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*) in the intermediate states and so forth;
they arise even without joy in the formless realms from the third dhyāna upward.
Alternatively, those pure qualities that exist in them are devoid of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and pliancy (*prasrabdhi*). (6.62–63)
The stream, the ford, the path, celibacy, the boat, and the chariot;
purgation which destroys the humors, and the ointment have been taught.
Whether it be a coarse sign or one that indicates tranquility—(6.64 [271])
The wise person should correctly grasp this and indeed practice it.
(6.65) The yogi should discern the proper times for tranquility, exertion, and equanimity, as well as their respective signs, in due order. (6.66)
Skill in entering, remaining in, and emerging from meditative attainments,
as well as constant and respectful application, is highly praised.
Alternatively, one who is self-arisen or has seen reality attains liberation.
Cultivating the sign, the wise ordinary person attains meditative absorption. (6.68) For those of dull intellect, the path is pleasant yet slow; likewise, it is painful for them.
For those of sharp intellect, it is swift; and similarly, there is another [path] beginning with the "unendurable" (akṣamā). (6.69)

Contentment with robes, alms-food, and even bedding and seats—these are the noble lineages characterized by non-greed; they consist of delighting in abandonment and finding joy therein. (6.70) The sixth chapter, the Compendium of the Path, is completed. Ṛbha.
